body: I'm also confused as how to handle a rejected promise in this case. Documentation regarding APP_INITIALIZER is not the best.

I believe (at least for the error above) is occurring because you passed an empty `reject()`.
If you pass something to it `reject('etc etc');`, the above error will go away, *but* the Application will still *not* bootstrap successfully.

Ideally when using `APP_INITIALIZER`, you want to have some sort of "backup" for when errors occur.  Let's say you called an API to get a JSON configuration that your application needs, in the `catch` try using `resolve({ /* basic app data */}` so that the application can start up (at least with some vague/basic data), you can attempt to fetch the correct data again later after bootstrapping. At least this way, you'll have the application starting up.
I definitely wouldn't want the app to continue starting when APP_INITIALIZER returns a rejected promise.

@StevenLiekens ... promise rejection is a signal for your app to behave due to that situation ... like route to some component that will explain a user the situation and so ... that's why it is a controlled state.
The way I see it, apps should not start unless they can be initialized successfully. Is that unreasonable?

@StevenLiekens ... but the formulation `initialized successfully` has a virtual sense ... what is it exactly? You can write code that uses positive / negative logic ... check many other conditions and there are many cases when both `resolve / reject` represents successful initialization in fact.
So how would you handle rejected promises? You can't return anything from an APP_INITIALIZER. How would you even know that it was rejected, let alone why?
That then() runs while the app is still doing the app_initializer phase. That's not the right place and time for redirecting to an error page or executing retry logic.

@StevenLiekens ... it was not meant to do it synchronously but emit something for later use when app is instantiating the main component. And also `APP_INITIALIZER` is `multi` provider so you can have more of them and you may need to decide on all their results if to continue and how and how to react to a user.

What you're describing sounds like a lot of custom code. Angular doesn't provide anything that could help us out with that.
I really don't want ignoring rejected promises to become the default behavior without better framework support for handling rejections.

@StevenLiekens ... yep, agree. Both `resolve / reject` as `multi` providers could be seen somehow similar as `validators` on top of the whole app and have them accessible via DI to any other place ... so it can react accordingly then?
